an0101.user: Snacks brand, email-led. I want the sharp, non-obvious read. Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,700, margin 50%, CAC ₹347, ROAS 4.9, 90-day repeat 11%, CTR 2.3%. Acquisition looks fantastic and I'm itching to scale — what am I missing?

What you're missing is hiding in plain sight at the end of your own numbers, and it's the whole game for a snacks brand: 11% repeat.

First, you're right about acquisition — first-order contribution = ₹1,700 × 50% − ₹347 = ₹850 − ₹347 = +₹503. Cheap CAC, 4.9 ROAS, strong CTR. The front of the machine is genuinely excellent, so I won't pretend otherwise.

But snacks is a consumption category — people finish the packet and should buy again within weeks. 11% repeat over 90 days means 89 of every 100 customers eat your product once and never return. That's not a small inefficiency; it's the entire long game leaking out the bottom. Your lifetime value barely clears that single ₹503, when for snacks it should be a multiple of it through reorders.

Here's the sharp part: that fantastic ROAS is precisely what makes scaling now a trap. Pour budget in and you buy more first orders at a rising CAC, none of them compounding — filling a bucket with no bottom, faster and more expensively. The acquisition metrics flatter a business that forgets its customers.

So the highest-leverage move is the opposite of scaling: fix repeat first. Why doesn't someone who liked the snack reorder? Build a replenishment nudge timed to run-out, a subscribe-and-save, a sampler-to-favourite flow. Move 11% toward 30% and the same spend pays you two and three times. Earn the repeat, then scale the acquisition you've already nailed.

an0103.user: Eyewear brand, Amazon Ads, I'm new. Let me describe it — my ads were doing well and now they just feel tired, like performance is slowly draining away and I'm not sure why. What should I look at?
an0103.assistant:
'Tired' is a real, measurable thing in ads, so let's confirm it rather than guess. Pull these:

- Your ad frequency. This is the giveaway. Above ~2.5 means the same people keep seeing the same ad, and they stop responding — at 3+ that 'draining away' feeling is almost certainly fatigue. Under 2, the audience is still fresh and something else is going on.
- The CTR trend over the last 4–6 weeks. A CTR drifting down as frequency climbs is the exact signature of a worn-out creative. A flat CTR points elsewhere.

Line up frequency next to the CTR trend. If frequency's high and CTR's sliding, your instinct is right and the fix is fresh creative with new angles — plus rotating in a new ad before the next one tires. If frequency's low, send those numbers back and we'll look at a different cause. One quick check settles it.

an0104.user: Amazon marketplace seller, running Meesho ads too. Narrow question — why is my CTR low? Last 30 days: 1.32M impressions, 18,892 clicks so CTR ~1.4%, but only 127 orders, a 0.67% conversion rate. AOV ₹800. On broad-match keywords.
an0104.assistant:
Your CTR is fine at 1.4% — the number quietly destroying you is the 0.67% conversion, and it's about who's clicking, not how many.

18,892 clicks for 127 orders means nearly nineteen thousand people clicked and walked. That's an intent problem. Broad-match is throwing your ad across loosely related searches, so you're paying for a flood of browsers who were never going to buy. And at an ₹800 AOV, you genuinely cannot afford that — every wasted click eats a product whose whole price is small to begin with.

Lifting CTR would only buy you more of these wrong clicks faster. The lever runs the other way: drop broad-match, move to phrase and exact on real purchase intent — the specific product terms where someone is actively shopping, not researching. Add a hard negative-keyword list to block the junk queries draining budget on every click. Your click volume will fall and your conversion rate will rise, which at ₹800 AOV is exactly the trade that makes the account work.

Stop optimising for clicks. Track cost per order instead — at this price point, qualified traffic is the only kind you can afford.

It's noise, and the fact that you paused to ask instead of overhauling already puts you ahead of most. Let me show you why this isn't a signal.

A 20% conversion-rate swing on 79 conversions is well inside normal variance. With a sample that small, a dozen orders shifting between one week and the next — a slow Monday, a couple of buyers who deliberated an extra day — moves the rate 20% on its own, with nothing actually changing underneath. You're looking at the statistical weather, not the climate.

The discipline that separates operators from tinkerers is exactly this: don't react to a percentage without asking whether the sample is large enough for it to mean anything. At 79 conversions, it isn't. Overhaul now and you'd reset Amazon's learning, trigger a genuine two-week dip while it recalibrates, and manufacture the very decline you were trying to prevent — the classic whipsaw.

What would actually count as signal: the conversion rate moving in the same direction for 3–4 consecutive weeks, or a single drop big enough to clear the noise floor — think 35–40%+ on this volume, not 20%. Hold everything steady, log the rate weekly, and reassess in a month. Right now the correct, sophisticated move is to do nothing.
